title: CSV Row Counter: Records in a Paste
description: Count the data records in a pasted CSV with the CSV Row Counter — header excluded, blanks handled, no spreadsheet needed. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a six-line paste with one header line counts 5 records — or 6, if one city was pasted twice, which is exactly the kind of surprise this count exists to surface early.
quick_answer: The CSV Row Counter counts how many records sit in a small pasted CSV without opening a spreadsheet application. The first non-empty line is the header; the non-empty lines after it count as data rows — paste and read your dataset's size.

A header and five city rows count 5. Paste the same file after a merge gone wrong and 6 appears — the extra row is a duplicate the count cannot name but absolutely announces.
Empty lines do not count as records. A file padded with blank separators reads smaller here than its line count in a text editor — the honest discrepancy.

popular_table.note: One line per record is the convention. CSVs with quoted multi-line fields (an address spanning lines) break line-counting — those files need a real parser, and their row counts here will read high.

faq: Does the header count as a row?
No — the first non-empty line is treated as the header and excluded. What remains is the record count people actually mean.
What if there is no header?
Then the first data line is mistaken for a header and the count reads one low. Add a header line to your snippet when the file lacks one.
Skipped, not counted — a record is a non-empty line.
A quoted address spanning three lines counts as three by line logic. That is the known limit of the simple method, stated openly.
Twice, if present twice — counting is not deduplication. The deduplicator’s census separates unique from repeated.
Snippet-scale: thousands of lines paste happily. Whole warehouses belong to wc -l and scripts — which implement this same convention.
Windows line endings count identically; the carriage return is not a record.
